slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1930 and 1940 censuses interpolated to November 1936 (the 1930 "Mexican" race category folded back into white, as the 1940 census recoded it); men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states, citizens only, American Indians included as citizens since 1924; Black voters here, mostly in Northern cities, swing toward the Democrats from 1936; calibrated to certified 1936 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1930–1940 interpolation to November 1936, women 21+ outside the South, all enfranchised by the Nineteenth Amendment; turnout from the carried-forward women-to-men ratio, calibrated to each state's 1936 vote.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1930–1940 interpolation to November 1936, white adults (including Mexican-origin adults, listed separately in 1930) in the eleven former Confederate states; poll taxes remain in most (Louisiana repealed its in 1934); calibrated to certified 1936 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1930–1940 interpolation to November 1936, Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement by poll tax, literacy test and the white primary continues, so the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion; the few who vote share in the Black realignment toward the Democrats that begins in 1936.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1930–1940 interpolation to November 1936, foreign-born white adults who were not naturalized; no state let aliens vote.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1936 comes out as it did: Roosevelt wins, 523–8. The closest state was New Hampshire, which went to Roosevelt by 1.8 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1930 and 1940 census counts interpolated to 1936 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1936 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 33.6 million more adults vote. No state flips. Roosevelt wins, 523–8. The closest call is New Hampshire, which holds for Roosevelt by 3.9 points. Landon wins in 0 of 100 draws.
assumptions: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1936.
howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.
New voters borrow the behaviour of naturalized citizens of the same state and sex; Black voters outside the South.
The numbers: the 1930 and 1940 census counts interpolated to 1936 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1936 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: Those public works programs are doing real good for young people, keeping them out of trouble. The President seems to know what he's doing with the money.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: The governor says it's all waste and politics, but those CCC boys have been doing real work around here. I'm not sure what to believe, but at least something's being done for folks now.
women.controlQuote: The governor says it's all waste and politics, but those CCC boys have been doing real work around here. I'm not sure what to believe, but at least something's being done for folks now.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The governor says they're wasting our relief money, but I had work through the WPA. The Republicans had their chance and look what happened. I think I'll stick with what we've got.

A neighbour asks what this person will do on Tuesday, 3 November. Will they cast a ballot for president, and for which candidate?
Think about Tuesday's presidential election from where this person stands. How likely are they to vote, and which candidate would get their vote?

reading.summary: Quincy meeting discusses certifying workers on the Wakulla Land Utilization project; school staff listed.
Writer recalls cheap cider and cheap barrels; cider mills are crumbling away.
Article calls the social security act society's response to wage earners' insecurity.
Heavy rain and storms damage fruit and flood lowlands; Glastonbury cauliflower crop is record-sized.
Drought effects on food prices vary, with higher dairy, fruit and vegetable prices expected.
Flight by Mrs. Markham ends in partial failure; Workers Alliance calls a WPA strike.
Speaker rejects the pension act's assumption that Americans lack foresight; favors society's responsibility.
Editorial compares U.S. debt favorably with British and other debts relative to income.
Lists federal relief spending in New England states, including WPA and CCC expenditures.
Governor criticizes federal relief spending as wasteful and political, and demands sweeping publicity.
Martin announces new auto union local at Baltimore's Fisher Body and Chevrolet plants.
Litchfield driver loses his false teeth along with his ice cream cone while swerving.
Works Progress Administration nursery schools employ needy women and serve over 1,000 Minnesota children.
Editorial defends the CCC as an investment in youth and expects debt repayment.
State Department survey describes reciprocal trade agreements and their effect on North Carolina.
CIO organizing worries employers, who are advised to close plants; AFL efforts earlier failed.
A union financial secretary reports full membership, recognition and raises, and backs the CIO.
Advertisement argues the national debt is manageable and taxes buy more now.
